prize_parts.citation: For the invention of base editors, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand breaks

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B009 to B008, with Liu alone. My own standard is that the work must be a game-changer that has already shown real consequences, and the chair's question on degraders forces me to apply it to my own first choice. Nobody on the committee, including me, can point to a widely approved degrader, so for B009 the consequences are still promised, not delivered. B008 meets the same bar on the chemistry: a deaminase directed to one nucleotide converts C to T or A to G in the genome without a double-strand break, which is a new chemical outcome and not a better way of cutting. The adenine base editor required evolving a deaminase that did not exist for DNA, which is a real invention and not a routine adaptation. Independent groups have reproduced it widely, and base editors are already in clinical use. Credit to Liu alone is the cleanest attribution available on the list: he conceived the programme and directed both editor families, and a single name leaves the committee no three-person boundary to defend. The question of what is new relative to 2020 has a direct answer: that prize honoured programmable cleavage, and this one honours programmable chemistry on a base with the cut deliberately removed.
statement.case_against: Three weaknesses remain, and I do not dismiss them. First, the clinical record is short, and bystander editing and off-target deamination are real open points, so the maturity argument I used against B009 applies in weaker form here. Second, a Liu-only prize leaves out Komor and Gaudelli, who did the hands-on work on the cytosine and adenine editors, and the concurrent Nishida and Kondo cytidine-deaminase fusion is a genuine independent early report that a one-name citation does not acknowledge. Third, a committee may still read this as a follow-on to the CRISPR prize. If the committee decides that priority cannot be defended with Liu alone, I would rather revert to the safer and fully mature B011 than to a three-name B008 with a contested third member.

responses.point: Chabes holds that Komor and Gaudelli made distinct inventions, the cytosine and the adenine editor, and that Liu alone hides this.
responses.response: I still read it differently. Komor and Gaudelli were first authors in a laboratory whose programme and design logic Liu set, and the Nobel tradition credits the conception and leadership of the programme, not each trainee who executed a step. I grant that the adenine editor required a fundamentally new evolved enzyme, which is the strongest point for naming Gaudelli. However, a three-name B008 reopens the Nishida and Kondo priority question, because if the committee names two trainees it is hard to justify leaving out an independent group that reported the first cytidine deaminase fusion. Liu alone is the narrowest defensible citation, and I would accept Liu, Komor and Gaudelli only if the committee prefers to honour the experimental invention over the programme.

responses.point: Somfai argues that C-N coupling needed its own ligand and mechanistic solutions that the 2010 laureates did not supply, and that decades of adoption beat dramatic clinical stories.
responses.response: This answers my round-1 novelty worry better than I expected. If Buchwald and Hartwig supplied the ligand design that made amine coupling general, and the 2010 laureates did not work on C-N bond formation, then B011 is a distinct achievement and not a continuation. My remaining question for Peter is what the mid-1990s work supplied that the Kosugi tin-amide coupling lacked: if the answer is catalytic amine coupling with free amines and a general ligand-controlled mechanism, I regard the Kosugi precedent as a footnote. I rank B011 above B009 now, and I keep it as my first alternative because it is the least contested on attribution, though I still see B008 as the newer chemistry.

responses.point: Linke proposes the two-part B011 plus B008 configuration, with Liu alone for base editing, and worries that the two parts are uneven in maturity.
responses.response: I agree that Liu alone is the right credit for base editing, and I note that we now agree on the pivotal point. I am still not persuaded by the pairing. A mature 1990s synthetic method and an early clinical genome technology do not tell one story, and the three-name allowance is used up by B011 and Liu. I would prefer one coherent part that the committee can defend line by line than two parts in which the weaker one drags the other. If the committee insists on two parts, Linke's pairing is the only one among those proposed that I can defend, because both parts have clean attribution.

responses.point: Aili would not choose B009 ahead of B016 this year, because lipid nanoparticles have already delivered approved medicines while degraders are still promised.
responses.response: I now accept the timing half of that argument and have acted on it. Where I stay apart is attribution for B016, because a trio inevitably omits MacLachlan, Madden or Langer, and Aili's own trio of Cullis, Hope and Anderson moved MacLachlan out after the opening exchange, while Sparr names Madden instead, which tells me the credit is not settled. The 2023 Medicine prize leaves the delivery question open, as Sparr argues, so I do not consider B016 poorly motivated. I keep it out of my alternatives only because I cannot name a trio I could defend, and I would reconsider if the committee agrees on one narrow citation.

responses.point: Brzezinski asks for evidence that the degrader record has reached a validated principle, and notes that PROTAC design and the cereblon mechanism are separate strands.
responses.response: My answer to the chair's question, which Peter also posed, is that it has not yet reached that point. The principle is real, with ternary complex structures and cereblon degradation data supporting it, but a prize standard that asks for consequences already shown is not met while no degrader is widely approved. A single citation could technically cover both strands, for example induced proximity, but that is a framing that hides two separate discovery histories, with Handa and Ito on one side and Crews and Deshaies on the other. I therefore withdraw B009 as my preferred part and keep it as a later candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts Liu alone, given Komor, Gaudelli and the independent Nishida and Kondo report, or whether priority forces a wider citation that I would find harder to defend.
Whether base editing is read as chemistry distinct from the 2020 cleavage prize, or as protein engineering close to it, which is Somfai's concern and I cannot fully rule it out.
Whether B009 will be validated by an approved degrader within a few years, which would change my ranking, and whether the PROTAC and glue strands can be written as a single citation.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B008, B011 or B009 is apparent from my profile. My Warshel and EVB connection and the Uppsala ribosome community are unrelated to these candidates, and I have no institutional tie to Liu, Buchwald, Hartwig, Crews, Deshaies or Handa. This is unchanged from round 1.
